extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of cultural studies, media studies, and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for doing and assessing cultural studies scholarship — centering ideological analysis, situating work in national traditions, and negotiating positivist and phenomenological resistances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root scholarship in native social formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses that do not develop roots on native grounds are simply a pose, another way of being an 'observer.' Voices from other contexts must be embedded in and deeply connected with the lines of discourse and the canons of evidence and argument decipherable only within the social, political, and intellectual traditions of given national social formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importing theories (e.g., Weber, Marx, Continental theory) is acceptable only when tied to national traditions and local canons of evidence; avoid detached, purely 'observer' stances. Examples: UK/British vs US differences in use of Weber and structuralism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center cultural studies on ideological analysis (neo-Marxist framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural studies should be centered on ideological analysis within a neo-Marxist framework — making ideology synecdochical of culture and examining how ideological forms mask and sustain the social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stuart Hall's approach is cited as exemplary: theoretically, historically, and empirically elegant; draws on Marxism and structuralism yet remains attentive to national limitations. Be aware this stance may provoke resistance in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the passive 'observer' pose — undertake explicit intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the pose of the detached observer; instead, explicitly use intelligence to change, modify, or reconstruct the social order when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one objects to cultural studies, the answer is not retreat but to analyze articulations among theory, practice, and ideology and to undertake active, explicit work rather than merely describing phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit ideological and political commitments (in sciences and humanities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The behavioral and positive sciences (and all intellectual vocabularies) should make explicit their own ideological implications and persuasions and defend them on their own ground rather than pretending that 'science says.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: pretending objectivity without acknowledging political implications. Positive sciences should analyze ideology beyond crude forms and state their moral/political commitments openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify problems produced by ideologies/theories and devise exits
rubrics_metrics.description: The task is to see the characteristic kinds of difficulties our ideologies and our theories (and our culture) get us into, then to try to devise ways of getting out of those difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological emphasis on diagnosing the dilemmas (e.g., reconciling individual desires with democratic demands) and crafting strategies rather than asserting final truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductionisms (culture ≠ ideology; diversity ≠ class-only analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce culture to ideology, social conflict to class conflict, consent to compliance, action to reproduction, or communication to coercion; maintain analytic complexity and phenomenological diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include treating ideology as an a priori total explanation or flattening diverse experiences into a single narrative of power. Balance attention to structure and to subjective diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate power and domination into phenomenological accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomenological approaches should not refuse to move power, conflict, and domination to the center of analysis; they must recognize those phenomena even while valuing subjective diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenomenologists often emphasize experience and 'structure of feeling' but should still examine forms of power and authority; failure to do so risks ignoring central social dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sciences as cultural practices
rubrics_metrics.description: All forms of practice and expression, including science, are cultural forms and should be analyzed as such — plunge science more deeply into culture and ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the notion that science occupies an Archimedean, ideology-free vantage point. Example guidance: analyze how scientific authority can function as class closure (Weber) or ideological practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mass media as a site for general social theory questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Center the mass media as a site (not a subject or a discipline) on which to engage the general question of social theory: how societies produce, reproduce, maintain, and transform themselves through communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass media should be treated as revealing moments of conflict, contradiction, and reproduction — useful for theorizing about social integration, crisis, and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute an outmoded philosophy of science for cultural analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural studies offers the advantage of abandoning an outmoded philosophy of science (maybe even dispensing with philosophy of science altogether) in favor of centering ideological and cultural analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits a focus on plural vocabularies and political commitments rather than on defending a single method as guarantor of truth. But be aware of critiques that this may appear moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance attention to master contradictions and everyday contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Address both major structural contradictions (race, class, gender) and 'garden-variety' contradictions (e.g., competition for positional goods in education) as integral to social life and curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses should examine how both macro and micro contradictions operate and reproduce social structures; removing one set of contradictions will produce new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize theoretical influences; avoid uncritical imports
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical currents (e.g., French structuralism, continental theory, symbolic interactionism, Weberian concepts) must be appropriated with attention to their fit and limits within a given national or disciplinary context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: uncritical adoption of structuralism in the US where other formalisms dominate; good practice: synthesize influences while respecting local intellectual traditions and empirical canons.
